The Self-Destructive Decline of the ‘Ulama: A Counterproductive Competition to Undermine One Another!

*Fard qā’im rabt-e millat se hai, tanhā kuchh nahīñ*

*Mauj hai daryā meñ aur bāhar-e daryā kuchh nahīñ*

***

The ‘Ulama are the guiding lights of society. People look to them for the cultivation of truth and goodness, lessons in justice and fairness, and the development of moral character and human values. Their knowledge, wisdom, conduct, and way of life are expected to serve as exemplary models for ordinary people to follow. It is only natural that people should be inspired by their example and drawn towards truth, justice, fairness, and morality.

Unfortunately, the reality in our society often falls short of these expectations.

Regrettably, the words, conduct, and mutual relationships of a section of the ‘Ulama have increasingly become subjects of public concern and criticism. Questions are being raised about their sense of propriety, moral character, decorum, and courtesy. Some have even become objects of public ridicule, while their exchanges and activities frequently provide material for entertainment on social media.

When the conduct of a group from whom society expects moral and spiritual refinement gives rise to such reactions, it is undoubtedly a matter of serious concern.

It is undeniable that differences exist among the ‘Ulama in their intellectual orientations, ideologies, interpretations, and approaches. Such differences are nothing new in the history of Islamic scholarship. Indeed, differences arising from Ijtihad and interpretation are a natural and integral part of scholarly engagement.

However, the expression and discussion of differences of opinion are also governed by certain principles, etiquettes, and intellectual disciplines. One may disagree with an opinion, point out flaws in its reasoning, or even describe a particular position as erroneous or unacceptable. None of these, however, justifies personal attacks, hostility, derogatory remarks, or attempts to humiliate those holding opposing views.

Unfortunately, a section of our ‘Ulama community does not adequately observe these principles and etiquettes when engaging with differences of opinion. Instead, an attitude of extreme self-satisfaction with one's own views and positions is often evident. *Kullu hizbin bimā ladayhim fariḥūn*—every group rejoices in what it has. This one-sided mindset, according to which only one's own group stands firmly upon the truth while others are regarded as false, misguided, or astray, is making mutual relationships increasingly intolerant and confrontational.

In Bangladesh, the ‘Ulama community can broadly be seen as divided into several major orientations. These include: (1) the Qawmi tradition; (2) the Barelvi tradition; (3) the Ahl-e Hadith tradition; (4) scholars associated with various Sufi shrines and Tariqahs outside the aforementioned three traditions; and (5) the Jamaat-oriented ‘Ulama, among whom scholars from several other traditions, except the Barelvi tradition, are also represented to varying degrees.

It is worth noting that each of these orientations has its own followers, supporters, and admirers. Although they differ in numerical strength, each has a certain degree of influence and standing in society.

The unfortunate reality is that an unhealthy sense of rivalry often prevails among these different orientations. Mutual antagonism and hostility are also evident among their respective followers. Rather than appreciating one another's activities, statements, and positions in a positive light, there are frequent attempts to portray them negatively. Consequently, a significant portion of the knowledge, intellect, effort, time, and organizational resources that should be devoted to the greater welfare of the Ummah, the country, and the nation is being squandered in internal disputes and conflicts.

The greatest damage resulting from this is that the collective capacity of the ‘Ulama to address society's broader moral and ideological crises is steadily weakening. The spread of irreligion, hostility towards religion, moral degeneration, obscenity, injustice, and inhumanity are issues that require the ‘Ulama to speak collectively and play an effective role.

The reality, however, is that in many instances, they regard scholars from outside their own respective circles as greater adversaries than these common challenges themselves. As a result, distance and distrust are emerging even in areas where a minimum degree of consensus and cooperation should prevail.

By continuously exhausting their energies in internal disputes, they are gradually losing the strength, capacity, and moral resolve needed to confront broader social and moral crises, religious hostility, and irreligion.

It must, of course, also be acknowledged that every one of these orientations has its share of knowledgeable, thoughtful, refined, wise, and genuinely concerned scholars who care deeply about the Ummah. Their scholarly pursuits, responsible statements, and constructive contributions extend beyond their immediate circles and are important for society at large.

At the same time, every orientation also has individuals whose words and conduct reveal considerable deficiencies in propriety, courtesy, decorum, and restraint. The scholarly competence of some is also seriously questionable. Their statements frequently display tendencies towards exaggeration, indiscretion, and transgression of proper limits.

Such individuals not only damage the public image of the wider ‘Ulama community but also become a source of embarrassment and harm to their own respective traditions. These tendencies are not confined to any particular group—whether Qawmi, Barelvi, Ahl-e Hadith, or Jamaat-oriented scholars. They are present, to varying degrees, across all these orientations. Therefore, criticism must be free from sectarian or group-based bias and grounded instead in principled and objective judgement.

On various occasions, I have personally drawn attention, either directly or indirectly, through social media to such deviations and inconsistencies within the ‘Ulama community. I have also written about the statements and activities of several contemporary public figures. In this connection, I have expressed my observations regarding certain statements and activities of Mufti Amir Hamza, MP, and Mawlana Tariq Munawar. I have even raised questions about the marketing and promotional strategies adopted for Dr. Mizanur Rahman Azhari's book *Ek Nojore Qur'an* (The Qur'an at a Glance). I have also expressed my observations and raised questions regarding the position taken by Mawlana Abdul Malek, the respected Khatib of Baitul Mukarram National Mosque, on the issue of the referendum.

The purpose of these discussions has never been to belittle any individual or particular orientation. Rather, it has been to create an environment conducive to necessary self-criticism and reform concerning principles, decorum, intellectual responsibility, and academic integrity. The recognition that no individual or group is above criticism needs to be firmly established within the ‘Ulama community as well.

In my view, expecting all differences of opinion among the ‘Ulama to disappear is unrealistic. Such differences existed in the past, exist in the present, and will continue to exist in the future. It is neither possible nor realistic to eliminate entirely the diversity of religious interpretations, intellectual positions, and adopted approaches.

Moreover, in today's religiously and ideologically diverse society and under a democratic system of governance, everyone has the right to express their own opinions. Simply disagreeing with someone's ideas or statements does not justify attempts to curtail that person's right to freedom of expression. Therefore, scholars from every orientation should present their respective views, ideas, and positions with supporting textual and rational evidence. However, they should do so while maintaining mutual respect, regard, and intellectual courtesy—not through an aggressive, hostile, or vindictive approach.

It is particularly important to remember that differences of opinion should never turn into factionalism; factionalism should never turn into enmity; and enmity should never escalate into confrontation and conflict. Despite differences of opinion, it is possible to create opportunities for mutual understanding, cooperation, and peaceful coexistence in the greater interest of all. In particular, where the ‘Ulama share common concerns and positions, they need to come closer to one another in the interests of the Ummah, the country, and the nation. It is not necessary to agree on everything. Rather, giving priority to collective action in areas where consensus is possible should be their foremost concern.

Regrettably, however, in recent times, mutual hostilities in certain instances have reached such a level that one group has come to regard another as its adversary. One group has attempted to obstruct the religious gatherings and programmes organized by another; some have even announced their intention to prevent their counterparts from holding such events. But if I announce today that I will prevent someone else's programme, what assurance do I have that tomorrow that person or their followers will not announce retaliatory measures against my programme? It is not difficult to foresee where the situation may ultimately lead if this cycle of reciprocal obstruction continues.

Such tendencies are deeply alarming. Their consequences will not be limited merely to the deterioration of relations between the parties concerned. Rather, they will further undermine the social acceptance, moral authority, and public trust enjoyed by the ‘Ulama as a whole.

In a society where the mutual conduct of the ‘Ulama itself becomes an example of intolerance and confrontation, the effectiveness of their moral teachings and advice will naturally come under question.

A fundamental point needs to be understood here: excesses, erroneous statements, or undesirable activities by scholars belonging to any particular orientation may certainly be challenged and criticized. Where necessary, even strong, evidence-based criticism may be warranted.

However, obstructing one another's religious gatherings and programmes, attempting to counter them by organizing rival gatherings and programmes, or adopting strategies to socially marginalize opposing groups cannot provide any lasting solution. On the contrary, such measures may further complicate the situation and make it increasingly confrontational. They also risk undermining freedom of expression, mutual tolerance, and social harmony.

It should be remembered that the greatest casualties of disputes among the ‘Ulama are their own social standing and moral credibility. The respect, trust, and expectations that people have towards them are not easily restored once they have been damaged.

On the other hand, the internal divisions among the ‘Ulama create opportunities for injustice, obscenity, hostility towards religion, moral degeneration, and inhumanity to spread further in various spheres of society. When the ‘Ulama exhaust their strength and resources by constantly pursuing disputes against one another, they not only weaken themselves but also lose their capacity to fulfil their responsibilities towards the wider Ummah and society.

Therefore, the most urgent priorities before the ‘Ulama community today are:

To keep differences of opinion within the bounds of normal scholarly discourse, maintain mutual respect and proper etiquette, and expand avenues of cooperation in matters of common interest and shared challenges. They must rise above identities such as which tradition one belongs to, whose follower one is, or which ideology one represents, and give priority to the interests of the wider Ummah, the country, and the nation.

For the strength of the ‘Ulama does not lie in their mutual conflicts; rather, it lies in their knowledge, moral integrity, wisdom, sense of responsibility, and collective contributions towards the common good.

In this connection, a meaningful couplet by Allama Muhammad Iqbal is worth recalling:

*Fard qā’im rabt-e millat se hai, tanhā kuchh nahīñ*

*Mauj hai daryā meñ aur bāhar-e daryā kuchh nahīñ*

**Meaning:**

As an individual, I am nothing in isolation; my strength, dignity, and fulfilment lie in my connection with the wider Millah and in mutual cooperation. Isolation and division do not make anyone genuinely stronger or more dignified. Rather, they fragment and weaken collective strength on the one hand, while undermining the individual's own strength and standing on the other.

Just as a wave possesses its existence, strength, and beauty only so long as it remains connected to the ocean, once separated from the ocean, it has no independent existence of its own.

The same principle applies equally to the ‘Ulama. Despite differences of opinion, maintaining mutual relationships, extending cooperation, and playing a united role in the greater interest of the Ummah enhance an individual's honour and dignity while simultaneously strengthening the collective strength and social acceptance of the ‘Ulama as a whole.
